summary: Describes the interface between the Mail Transfer Protocol software and the NIMAIL mail system in the ISI TOPS-20 implementation. It is a companion to the main implementation description.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo explains the doorway where two mail programs pass letters to one another on the same computer.

questions: how does mtp send mail to nimail
subtitle: How MTP and NIMAIL exchange mail on ISI TOPS-20.

tldr.problem: The Mail Transfer Protocol and the Network Independent Mail system needed a way to exchange messages on the same TOPS-20 computer, with automatic translation of address formats.
tldr.mechanism: NIMAIL sends mail to MTP using the RFC 785 file format. MTP sends mail back to NIMAIL in files that convert the source address to NIMAIL format and restructure destination addresses with route information.
tldr.outcome: The two systems could interoperate seamlessly, with each handling address translation transparently.

today: RFC 786 describes a historical interface for TOPS-20 systems in the early 1980s. Both MTP and NIMAIL are no longer in use, and this specification is primarily of archival interest.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 786 defines how the Mail Transfer Protocol (MTP) and the Network Independent Mail (NIMAIL) system exchange messages on ISI's TOPS-20 system. NIMAIL is a mail system based on NIFTP (the Network Independent File Transfer Protocol), documented in IEN 169. This RFC specifies the file interface, address transformations, and directory conventions.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is about two mail systems on the same computer and how they pass mail back and forth.

sections.title: Bidirectional Exchange
sections.content: Mail flows in two directions. When NIMAIL sends mail to MTP, it uses the file format from RFC 785: a control file pointing to a mail file, with FROM and TO addresses. When MTP sends mail to NIMAIL, it creates files with a different structure. MTP files contain a list of recipient addresses, followed by a Via: line with the sending host and timestamp (in TOPS-20 format dd-mmm-yy hh:mm:ss), followed by mail headers and body. Files are named arbitrarily with a .NIMAIL.-1 extension and placed in the NIMAIL directory.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail going in can be in one format, and mail going out can be in another. Each system transforms the address list so the other understands it.

sections.title: Address Format Conversion
sections.content: NIMAIL uses a source-routed address format with percent signs and a final host, such as joe%hostx%hosty%hostz@isie. When NIMAIL sends to MTP, this becomes FROM: <NIMAIL@ISIE> and TO: <@hostz,@hosty,joe@hostx> in MTP path format. Conversely, when MTP sends to NIMAIL an address like FROM: <sam@SRI-NIC> with TO: <@ISIE,@hostz,@hosty,joe@hostx>, it becomes joe%hostx%hosty@hostz with Via: ISIE in the NIMAIL file. The key constraint is that all addresses in a single NIMAIL file from MTP must share the same final @host part.
sections.plainLanguage: MTP uses angle brackets and route symbols, NIMAIL uses percent signs. The two systems automatically translate between the two styles.
